title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
This page provides variable-level diagnostics for all 175 numeric variables in the PDET panel (170 municipalities, 2000–2025).






NoteHow to read the diagnostic flags





Each category tab shows four things:

Summary statistics table – searchable table with N, % missing, % zero, mean, median, SD, skewness, municipality coverage, and year range. The is_static column marks variables with zero within-municipality variation across years (these cannot be used in fixed-effects models).
Diagnostic flags – automatic alerts for:

Zero-inflated (>50% zeros): Most observations are zero; the variable measures rare events. Consider a binary indicator or hurdle model.
High missingness (>50% NA): The variable covers less than half the panel. Missingness is likely MAR (conditional on year or department) – see the Data Audit page.
Highly skewed (|skew| > 3): Distribution has a very long right tail. Log(1 + x) transformation strongly recommended before regression.
Static (no within-muni variation): Value is identical across all years for each municipality. Cannot be used as outcome in panel FE models; useful only as cross-sectional moderator.
Low coverage (<100 munis): Fewer than 100 of 170 PDET municipalities have any data.
Short time span (<10 years): Limited temporal coverage.

Distributions – histograms for each variable. Zero-inflated variables will show a large spike at zero. Skewed variables will have long right tails.
Temporal trends – median value across municipalities by year. Dot size = number of municipalities with data that year. Flat lines = static variables. The 2016 vertical line (where shown) marks the Peace Agreement.










WarningVariables flagged for exclusion or recoding





Based on diagnostics, the following variables should be dropped or recoded before modeling:

P_investment_total_cop__art, P_n_projects_completed__art, P_n_pilars_covered__art – all zeros, failed extraction
P_impl_ceasefire_disarmament__art, P_impl_communication__art – >99% NA, near-zero/constant variance
S_n_cadastral_managers__igac – constant = 1, zero variance
G_land_cover_share__prio – near-constant (mean = 0.97), negligible variation
J_n_restitution_sentences__urt – constant = 1 for all observed rows, likely misspecified; verify source
V_homicides_q025__jep, V_homicides_q975__jep – redundant with mean (r ~ 1)
S_gdp_percapita_constant__dnp – only 5 years (2005-2009)
S_poverty_headcount__dnp – single year (2005), use as baseline control only

All other variables with >50% NA or high skew are usable with appropriate transformation and available-case estimation.





Show code
overview <- desc_table |>
  dplyr::group_by(Category = cat_labels[category]) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    `N vars`         = dplyr::n(),
    `Median % NA`    = round(median(pct_na), 1),
    `Median % zero`  = round(median(pct_zero, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    `N static`       = sum(is_static, na.rm = TRUE),
    `N high-skew`    = sum(abs(skewness) > 3, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Year range`     = paste0(min(year_min, na.rm = TRUE), "–", max(year_max, na.rm = TRUE)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Cross-Category Correlation


Show code
# Pick one representative variable per source for a manageable heatmap
rep_vars <- desc_table |>
  dplyr::group_by(source) |>
  dplyr::slice_max(n_obs, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::pull(variable)

if (length(rep_vars) >= 3) {
  cor_data <- panel |>
    dplyr::select(dplyr::all_of(rep_vars))

  cor_mat <- cor(cor_data, use = "pairwise.complete.obs", method = "spearman")

  # Clean names for display
  rownames(cor_mat) <- gsub("__.*", "", gsub("^[VPJSG]_", "", rownames(cor_mat)))
  colnames(cor_mat) <- gsub("__.*", "", gsub("^[VPJSG]_", "", colnames(cor_mat)))

  cor_long <- as.data.frame(as.table(cor_mat)) |>
    dplyr::rename(var1 = Var1, var2 = Var2, rho = Freq)

  ggplot(cor_long, aes(x = var1, y = var2, fill = rho)) +
    geom_tile(color = "white") +
    geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(abs(rho) > 0.3, sprintf("%.2f", rho), "")),
              size = 2) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b",
                          midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1),
                          name = "Spearman rho") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
    theme(
      axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 7),
      axis.text.y = element_text(size = 7),
      panel.grid = element_blank()
    ) +
    labs(title = "Cross-source Spearman correlations (one variable per source)",
         x = NULL, y = NULL)
}

title: Panel 3 · Regression Models
text:
NoteAbout this panel: Why spatial regression?





Standard OLS assumes observations are independent. For municipal-level data in Colombia this assumption fails: neighbouring municipalities share geography, armed group activity, state infrastructure, and economic conditions. Ignoring spatial dependence inflates standard errors and biases coefficient estimates.
This panel estimates four regression specifications of increasing complexity:








Model
What it assumes
When to use




OLS
No spatial dependence (baseline)
Benchmark only


SLM (Spatial Lag)
Outcome in municipality i depends on outcomes in neighbours (diffusion)
If peace/conflict spreads across borders


SEM (Spatial Error)
Unmeasured confounders are spatially correlated
If omitted variables cluster geographically


SDM (Spatial Durbin)
Both outcome and predictors have spatial spillovers
Most flexible; preferred if both effects are plausible



Current outcome: Log equity conciliators (log1p), a measure of local dispute resolution capacity. Key predictors: Ever-treated under the Peace Agreement, cumulative PDET investment, conflict exposure, basic needs deficit, population, terrain, indigenous territory coverage.
Spatial weights use Queen contiguity on the complete-case PDET subset. Residual maps show whether spatial patterns remain after conditioning on included predictors.

§3.4 Spatial Lag Model (SLM)






NoteWhat the SLM captures





The SLM adds a spatial lag of the outcome – a weighted average of neighbouring municipalities’ conciliator counts – to the right-hand side. A positive and significant spatial lag coefficient (rho) indicates that the outcome diffuses across municipal boundaries: municipalities adjacent to high-capacity ones tend to develop higher capacity themselves, possibly through shared state presence, referral networks, or spillover investment.





Show code
slm_fit <- NULL

if (!is.null(ols_fit) && exists("wts_cc") && !is.null(wts_cc) && !is.null(sf_cc)) {

  sf_model <- sf_cc |>
    dplyr::left_join(df_cc, by = "dane_code")

  slm_fit <- tryCatch({
    spatialreg::lagsarlm(
      formula_ols,
      data        = sf_model,
      listw       = wts_cc$lw,
      zero.policy = TRUE
    )
  }, error = function(e) {
    cat(glue::glue("SLM failed: {conditionMessage(e)}\n"))
    NULL
  })
}

if (!is.null(slm_fit)) {
  print(summary(slm_fit))

  # ── Residual map ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

    dplyr::mutate(resid = slm_resids)

§3.5 Spatial Error Model (SEM)






NoteWhat the SEM captures





The SEM models spatial dependence in the error term rather than the outcome itself. This is appropriate when the spatial clustering of residuals arises from omitted variables that are geographically correlated – for example, unmeasured differences in departmental-level governance quality, historical state presence, or cultural factors that vary across PDET subregions. The lambda coefficient measures the degree of spatial contagion in those unobservables.

text:
§3.6 Spatial Durbin Model (SDM)






NoteWhy the SDM and direct/indirect effects?





The SDM nests both the SLM and SEM as special cases. It adds spatially lagged predictors alongside the spatial lag of the outcome. This matters for interpretation: in the SLM, the coefficient on a predictor captures only the direct effect in municipality i. The SDM allows us to separately estimate:

Direct effect: impact of the predictor in i on the outcome in i (including feedback through the spatial lag)
Indirect effect: spillover to neighbouring municipalities j through the spatial multiplier
Total effect: direct + indirect

For a peacebuilding variable like cumulative PDET investment, finding a significant indirect effect would suggest that investment in one municipality improves dispute resolution capacity in its neighbours.





Show code
sdm_fit <- NULL

if (!is.null(ols_fit) && exists("wts_cc") && !is.null(wts_cc) && exists("sf_model")) {
  sdm_fit <- tryCatch({
    spatialreg::lagsarlm(
      formula_ols,
      data        = sf_model,
      listw       = wts_cc$lw,
      type        = "Durbin",
      zero.policy = TRUE
    )
  }, error = function(e) {
    cat(glue::glue("SDM failed: {conditionMessage(e)}\n"))
    NULL
  })
}

if (!is.null(sdm_fit)) {
  print(summary(sdm_fit))

  # ── Direct / Indirect / Total effects ────────────────────────────────────
  sdm_impacts <- tryCatch({
    spatialreg::impacts(sdm_fit, listw = wts_cc$lw, zero.policy = TRUE, R = 500)
  }, error = function(e) {
    cat(glue::glue("impacts() failed: {conditionMessage(e)}\n"))

text:
§3.8 Model Comparison






NoteInterpreting AIC and BIC





Lower AIC/BIC indicates better model fit penalised for complexity. Both criteria trade off goodness-of-fit against the number of parameters; BIC applies a stronger penalty for larger samples. For spatial models, a substantially lower AIC relative to OLS (difference > 4) confirms that accounting for spatial structure improves model performance. If SLM and SEM perform similarly, the SDM is preferred on theoretical grounds if spillover effects are plausible.





Show code
extract_fit_stats <- function(fit, label) {
  if (is.null(fit)) return(NULL)

  aic_val    <- tryCatch(AIC(fit),    error = function(e) NA_real_)
  bic_val    <- tryCatch(BIC(fit),    error = function(e) NA_real_)
  ll_val     <- tryCatch({
    ll <- logLik(fit)
    as.numeric(ll)
  }, error = function(e) NA_real_)
  nobs_val   <- tryCatch(nobs(fit),   error = function(e) NA_integer_)

  tibble::tibble(
    Model  = label,
    N      = nobs_val,
    LogLik = round(ll_val,  3),
    AIC    = round(aic_val, 3),
    BIC    = round(bic_val, 3)
  )
}

compare_tbl <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  extract_fit_stats(ols_fit, "OLS"),
  extract_fit_stats(slm_fit, "SLM"),
  extract_fit_stats(sem_fit, "SEM"),
  extract_fit_stats(sdm_fit, "SDM")
)

  non_na <- compare_tbl |> dplyr::filter(!is.na(AIC))
  if (nrow(non_na) > 1) {
    best_row  <- non_na[which.min(non_na$AIC), ]
    ols_aic   <- non_na$AIC[non_na$Model == "OLS"]
    delta_aic <- if (length(ols_aic) > 0) round(ols_aic - best_row$AIC, 2) else NA
    cat(glue::glue(
      "\nBest model by AIC: {best_row$Model} (AIC = {best_row$AIC})\n"
    ))
    if (!is.na(delta_aic) && best_row$Model != "OLS") {
      cat(glue::glue(
        "delta-AIC vs. OLS: {delta_aic} -- spatial model {ifelse(delta_aic > 4, 'substantially', 'marginally')} preferred.\n"
      ))
    }
  }
} else {
  cat("No model results available for comparison.\n")
}

NoteAbout this panel





This panel explores relationships between variables rather than the distribution of any single variable. Each section asks a different question:

§2.1 Scatterplots: Are conflict history and justice infrastructure correlated? Do municipalities with more peacebuilding investment have lower violence? Points are municipality means across all available years. Axes are log-scaled to handle extreme skew.
§2.2 Bivariate Moran’s I: Does the geographic neighbor of a high-conflict municipality also have low justice infrastructure? Bivariate spatial autocorrelation tests this.
§2.3 LISA Maps: Which specific municipalities drive the spatial clustering? High-High = conflict cluster; Low-Low = peaceful cluster; High-Low / Low-High = spatial outliers (interesting cases).
§2.4 MAUP Sensitivity: Does the spatial pattern depend on how we allocate UCDP events to municipal boundaries? This section tests robustness to different aggregation rules.

All spatial weights use Queen contiguity restricted to the 170 PDET municipalities.

Peace Atlas — PDET Colombia
text:
This site is the interactive deliverable for GEOG 560: Spatial Regression (Spring 2026). It is also the methodological groundwork for Chapter 1 of my dissertation, The Architecture of Peace, which examines how peacebuilding network structure shapes peace outcomes across Colombia’s most conflict-affected municipalities following the 2016 Peace Agreement.
The core question across all panels is: do municipal-level indicators of peace and institutional capacity in post-conflict Colombia cohere as a latent construct, or do they pick up fundamentally different things? And critically: how does their spatial distribution—clustering, regime structure, boundary sensitivity—inform or distort that answer?






NoteBackground: What are PDET municipalities?





Colombia’s 2016 Peace Agreement between the government and the FARC guerrilla established Programas de Desarrollo con Enfoque Territorial (PDET) – Territorial Development Programs with a Territorial Focus. The PDET framework designated 170 municipalities across 16 subregions as priority zones for post-conflict reconstruction based on four criteria: (1) high historical presence of armed conflict and illegal economies, (2) high poverty rates, (3) weak institutional presence, and (4) environmental or agricultural vulnerability.
These 170 municipalities – the unit of analysis throughout this site – are not a random sample. They are the municipalities where the state has historically been weakest, where armed groups have exercised the most governance, and where the peace agreement’s implementation faces the highest structural barriers. This matters for interpretation: low institutional indicators here reflect structural conditions, not just measurement error.

title: Peace Atlas — PDET Colombia
text:
This site is the interactive deliverable for GEOG 560: Spatial Regression (Spring 2026). It is also the methodological groundwork for Chapter 1 of my dissertation, The Architecture of Peace, which examines how peacebuilding network structure shapes peace outcomes across Colombia’s most conflict-affected municipalities following the 2016 Peace Agreement.
The core question across all panels is: do municipal-level indicators of peace and institutional capacity in post-conflict Colombia cohere as a latent construct, or do they pick up fundamentally different things? And critically: how does their spatial distribution—clustering, regime structure, boundary sensitivity—inform or distort that answer?






NoteBackground: What are PDET municipalities?





Colombia’s 2016 Peace Agreement between the government and the FARC guerrilla established Programas de Desarrollo con Enfoque Territorial (PDET) – Territorial Development Programs with a Territorial Focus. The PDET framework designated 170 municipalities across 16 subregions as priority zones for post-conflict reconstruction based on four criteria: (1) high historical presence of armed conflict and illegal economies, (2) high poverty rates, (3) weak institutional presence, and (4) environmental or agricultural vulnerability.
These 170 municipalities – the unit of analysis throughout this site – are not a random sample. They are the municipalities where the state has historically been weakest, where armed groups have exercised the most governance, and where the peace agreement’s implementation faces the highest structural barriers. This matters for interpretation: low institutional indicators here reflect structural conditions, not just measurement error.

Data Coverage


Show code
if (nrow(panel) > 0) {
  data_vars <- setdiff(names(panel), c("dane_code", "year"))
  numeric_vars <- data_vars[sapply(panel[data_vars], is.numeric)]

  # Count PDET municipalities with at least 1 non-NA value per variable
  coverage <- purrr::map_dfr(numeric_vars, function(v) {
    n <- panel |>
      dplyr::group_by(dane_code) |>
      dplyr::summarise(has = any(!is.na(.data[[v]])), .groups = "drop") |>
      dplyr::pull(has) |> sum()
    tibble::tibble(
      variable = v,
      n_munis  = n,
      category = dplyr::case_when(
        startsWith(v, "V_") ~ "Violence & Conflict",
        startsWith(v, "P_") ~ "Peacebuilding",
        startsWith(v, "J_") ~ "Justice & Dispute",
        startsWith(v, "S_") ~ "Socioeconomic",
        startsWith(v, "G_") ~ "Geographic",
        TRUE ~ "Other"
      ),
      source = sub(".*__", "", v)
    )
  })

  # Show top variables per category
  cat_colors <- c(
    "Violence & Conflict" = "#b2182b",
    "Peacebuilding"       = "#1b7837",
    "Justice & Dispute"   = "#2166ac",
    "Socioeconomic"       = "#8c510a",
    "Geographic"          = "#542788"
  )

  top_vars <- coverage |>
    dplyr::group_by(category) |>
    dplyr::slice_max(n_munis, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE) |>
    dplyr::ungroup()

  clean_label <- gsub("__.*", "", gsub("^[VPJSG]_", "", top_vars$variable))

  p <- ggplot(top_vars, aes(x = n_munis,
                             y = reorder(clean_label, n_munis),
                             fill = category)) +
    geom_col(width = 0.7) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 170, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = cat_colors, name = "Category") +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 180), expand = c(0, 0)) +
    facet_wrap(~category, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
    labs(x = "PDET municipalities with data (max = 170)", y = NULL,
         title = "Data Coverage: Top 5 Variables per Category") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    theme(legend.position = "none",
          strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
          panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
  p
}
